title: How do you solve a cost reduction case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete cost reduction case guide: mapping the cost base, sizing levers against a 15% target in a bank, the mistakes to avoid and practice prompts.
hook: You solve a cost reduction case by mapping where the money goes, attacking the biggest cost lines first, sizing each lever against the target, and then checking the net saving after new running costs and any damage to revenue. It is less about clever ideas than about discipline. This guide works through a bank's $150M savings target and shows why the gross number is never the answer.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet a cost reduction case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example: a bank cuts 15%
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

When you will meet a cost reduction case

The client needs to spend less, usually against a target: "cut operating costs by 15% in two years", "our logistics costs have doubled, what can we do?" Sometimes the case starts as a profitability problem and becomes a cost case once you find that revenue is fine. Operations cases (making a process faster or cheaper) overlap heavily, but they focus on one process rather than the whole cost base.

The structure, and the first question to ask

Ask about scope and constraints before you suggest a single cut:

Which costs are in scope, how much by when, and what must not suffer: quality, safety or service levels?

Then use a simple equation. Cost = how much we do × resources used per unit × price paid per resource. Each branch of the structure cuts one factor:

  • Need less. Stop an activity (close a branch, move to self-service) or do less of it (lower a service level, such as free next-day delivery).
  • Use less per unit. Cut waste and rework; get more output per person or machine.
  • Pay less per unit. Negotiate better prices, switch to cheaper inputs, or outsource.

Apply it to the biggest cost lines first, and protect the costs that bring in revenue, such as sales staff or the parts of service customers pay for. The cost reduction framework explains each branch, and the cost levers tip lists where to look across a business.

A fully worked example: a bank cuts 15%

The prompt: a retail bank spends $1B a year on operating costs and wants to cut 15%, or $150M, within two years, without hurting customer satisfaction. The numbers are illustrative.

Step 1: map the cost base

Ask for the costs by category before suggesting anything:

CategoryAnnual costShare
Branches$300M30%
IT$250M25%
Back office$200M20%
Call centres$150M15%
Other (property, HR, finance)$100M10%
Total$1,000M100%

Step 2: size realistic levers on the biggest lines

AreaLeverGross saving
Branches ($300M)Close the 20% with the lowest footfall$60M
Call centres ($150M)Move 30% of calls to the app and chat$45M
IT ($250M)Consolidate suppliers, cut 10%$25M
Back office ($200M)Automate routine processing, cut 10%$20M
Total$150M

Branches and call centres provide $105M, or 70% of the total, so that is where the detail matters most.

Step 3: build the net saving, not the gross

A list of gross savings almost always overstates what the client will see. Check three things:

  • New running costs. Handling 30% more queries in the app and chat is not free. Say that adds $5M a year.
  • Double counting. Automating the back office needs new software, which adds to the IT bill you have just cut. Say that is another $5M a year.
  • One-off costs. Redundancies, lease exits and system changes are paid once. They do not reduce the yearly saving, but they belong in the business case.

Net recurring saving: $150M − $5M − $5M = $140M, or 14%. The programme misses the target. That is more useful to tell the client than declaring victory on the gross figure. A fourth lever closes the gap: a 10% cut in "other" costs, through property consolidation and shared HR and finance, adds $10M and brings the total back to $150M.

Step 4: check what each cut does to revenue

Branch closures may lose some customers, especially older ones who rely on branches, so close only where digital use is already high and keep a route for complex needs such as mortgages. Call-centre savings only work if the app genuinely resolves those queries; otherwise customers call back, and costs and complaints both rise.

Step 5: the recommendation

We can reach $150M of net yearly savings with five levers. Branches and call centres provide most of it, but after the new costs of digital service and automation software, those four levers give $140M, so we also need about $10M from property and support functions. I'd start with IT suppliers and back-office automation, which carry the least customer risk, and close branches only where digital use is already high. The main risk is customer loss from branch closures, so I'd track satisfaction and account closures in the first wave before going further.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer starts cutting before it knows where the money goes:

They could cut travel, renegotiate with suppliers, freeze hiring and reduce marketing.

Travel and marketing may be a few percent of the cost base. A strong answer maps first and focuses:

Before suggesting cuts, I'd like to see the cost base by category so we can focus on the biggest lines.
Gross savings reach $150M, but net of new running costs we're at $140M, so we're $10M short.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Brainstorming before mapping the cost base. Ask for costs by category first.
  2. Spreading effort evenly. Spend your time on the lines that make up most of the cost.
  3. Cutting costs that bring in revenue. Sales staff and service quality often pay for themselves.
  4. Reporting gross savings. Subtract new running costs and overlaps, and list one-off costs separately.
  5. Not adding it up. Check the total against the target and say plainly if it falls short.

Practise with these prompts

Quick maths: a retailer spends $50M a year on fulfilment and wants a 10% saving. You find $2.4M in warehouse labour, $1.5M in transport and $1.5M in packaging. $0.4M of that is counted twice, and the changes add $0.3M of yearly running cost. Does it hit the target?

Show the answer

Gross: $2.4M + $1.5M + $1.5M = $5.4M, which looks like 10.8%. Net: $5.4M − $0.4M − $0.3M = $4.7M, or 9.4% of $50M. It misses the $5M target by $0.3M, so you need another lever or a conversation about the target.

A fashion retailer's online returns now cost $40M a year, double three years ago.

Show the answer
  • Number of returns: did online orders grow? Return rate by category, size and brand; serial returners.
  • Cost per return: shipping, handling, refurbishing; items that can no longer be sold.
  • Why customers return: fit and sizing, photos and descriptions, ordering several sizes on purpose.
  • Policy: free returns, the return window, charging, in-store returns, exchanges first.

Where to start: orders × return rate × cost per return. Find which grew, then the categories driving it.

The trap: listing policy changes before splitting the number of returns from the cost per return.

A food-delivery start-up is burning $5M a month. Where would you cut?

Show the answer
  • Unit economics per order: commission, delivery fee, courier cost, discounts and refunds.
  • Marketing: cost to acquire a customer against their value; promotions with no repeat orders.
  • Cities: profit by city; exit or pause the weakest.
  • Fixed costs: head office, tech, offices, hiring plans.

Where to start: profit per order by city. If every order loses money, more volume makes it worse.

The trap: cutting head office first when the loss is in every order.

Where to practise next

  • Run a full case: Cedarline Home (does the chatbot really handle 35% of customers?) or Coral Pharmacy (four warehouses into one).
  • Revise the opening: what to ask first in a cost or operations case, and the trap.
  • More prompts: 13 cost reduction questions.
